title: Demonstrate understanding of real and complex number systems

lessons.title: The real number system
lessons.html:
Classifying numbers

Numbers are organised into nested sets:

SetSymbolExamples
Natural numbersℕ1, 2, 3, ...
Whole numbersℕ₀0, 1, 2, ...
Integersℤ..., −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, ...
Rational numbersℚa/b with a, b integers, b ≠ 0: ¾, −2.5, 0.333...
Irrational numbers√2, π, e: non-terminating, non-recurring decimals
Real numbersℝAll rationals and irrationals

A rational number's decimal either terminates (0.25) or recurs (0.1666...). Irrational numbers cannot be written as fractions of integers.

Properties of real numbers

  • Closure: adding or multiplying two reals gives a real.
  • Commutative: a + b = b + a; ab = ba.
  • Associative: (a + b) + c = a + (b + c).
  • Distributive: a(b + c) = ab + ac.
  • Identity: a + 0 = a; a × 1 = a.
  • Inverse: a + (−a) = 0; a × (1/a) = 1 for a ≠ 0.

Surds, exponents and rounding

Surds such as √50 simplify: √50 = √25 × √2 = 5√2. Exponent laws: aᵐ × aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ, (aᵐ)ⁿ = aᵐⁿ, a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ, a^(1/n) = ⁿ√a.

In business, rounding matters. Interest calculations, VAT and conversion between kilograms and tonnes produce non-terminating decimals. Round only at the final step, and to an appropriate precision (cents for money). Rounding too early in a calculation over 1,000 tonnes of grain can make a noticeable difference to the invoice.

Where the reals fall short

The equation x² + 1 = 0 has no real solution, because the square of any real number is non-negative. This motivates the complex numbers.

lessons.title: Complex numbers and operations
lessons.html:
Defining i

Define the imaginary unit i with i² = −1. A complex number has the form z = a + bi, where a is the real part, Re(z), and b is the imaginary part, Im(z). The set of complex numbers is ℂ, and every real number is a complex number with b = 0.

Powers of i

i¹ = i, i² = −1, i³ = −i, i⁴ = 1, and the pattern repeats every four powers. So i¹⁰ = i⁸ × i² = −1.

Operations

  • Addition: (3 + 2i) + (1 − 5i) = 4 − 3i.
  • Subtraction: (3 + 2i) − (1 − 5i) = 2 + 7i.
  • Multiplication: (3 + 2i)(1 − 5i) = 3 − 15i + 2i − 10i² = 3 − 13i + 10 = 13 − 13i.
  • Conjugate: the conjugate of z = a + bi is z̄ = a − bi. Note z × z̄ = a² + b², a real number.
  • Division: multiply top and bottom by the conjugate of the denominator. (2 + i)/(1 − i) = (2 + i)(1 + i)/[(1 − i)(1 + i)] = (2 + 2i + i + i²)/2 = (1 + 3i)/2 = ½ + (3/2)i.

Equality

a + bi = c + di only if a = c and b = d. This lets you solve equations by comparing real and imaginary parts.

Solving quadratics

For ax² + bx + c = 0, x = [−b ± √(b² − 4ac)] / 2a. If the discriminant b² − 4ac < 0, the roots are complex conjugates.

Example: x² − 4x + 13 = 0. Discriminant = 16 − 52 = −36. √(−36) = 6i. x = (4 ± 6i)/2 = 2 ± 3i.

lessons.title: The Argand diagram and polar form
lessons.html:
Representing complex numbers

The Argand diagram plots z = a + bi as the point (a; b), with the real axis horizontal and the imaginary axis vertical. Addition of complex numbers corresponds to adding vectors.

Modulus and argument

  • Modulus: |z| = √(a² + b²), the distance from the origin.
  • Argument: arg z = θ, the angle from the positive real axis, with tan θ = b/a. Check the quadrant: for z = −1 + i, θ = 135° (3π/4), not −45°.

Example: z = 3 + 4i has |z| = 5 and θ = tan⁻¹(4/3) ≈ 53.1°.

Polar form

z = r(cos θ + i sin θ), where r = |z|. In polar form, multiplication and division are simple:

  • Multiply: moduli multiply and arguments add.
  • Divide: moduli divide and arguments subtract.
  • De Moivre's theorem: [r(cos θ + i sin θ)]ⁿ = rⁿ(cos nθ + i sin nθ).

Example: (1 + i)⁴. |1 + i| = √2, θ = 45°. So (1 + i)⁴ = (√2)⁴ (cos 180° + i sin 180°) = 4(−1 + 0i) = −4.

Why it matters

Complex numbers are used in electrical engineering (alternating current in irrigation pumps, motors and power systems), signal processing, control systems and the analysis of oscillating systems. A technician analysing the power factor of a centre-pivot motor uses the same algebra. Understanding the number systems also builds the reasoning needed for higher mathematics and technical work.

Key points

  • ℕ ⊂ ℤ ⊂ ℚ ⊂ ℝ ⊂ ℂ; irrationals are non-recurring, non-terminating decimals.
  • Round only at the final step of calculations.
  • i² = −1 and powers of i repeat every four.
  • Divide complex numbers by multiplying by the conjugate.
  • |z| = √(a² + b²); in polar form, moduli multiply and arguments add.
